knowledge.text: The current diff rewrites the ordinary non-desklamp search step as a single-pass sweep across distinct receptacle families: open each closed container once on reaching it, use recent observations to avoid returning to a receptacle just confirmed empty, and when one family (drawers, say) yields nothing, switch to a different uninspected family (cabinets, shelves, countertops/other surfaces, appliances) before revisiting any earlier location, keeping the sweep within the step budget. In three current pairs the Parent exhausted or looped one family and never reached the family holding the exact target, while the Candidate's broader sweep did reach it: in put-a-clean-butterknife-in-drawer the Parent opened drawers in sequence and never visited countertop 2 before the 50-step limit (P6:1, P6:2, P6:49, P6:50), whereas the Candidate crossed drawers, countertop 1 and cabinets, reached countertop 2, took the exact butterknife and placed it in 21 steps (Q6:4, Q6:16, Q6:17, Q6:21); in put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet the Parent cycled cabinets 1-4 and the sinkbasins and never visited shelf 1 (P8:6, P8:10, P8:50), whereas the Candidate added shelf 1 to its sweep, found and took the exact soapbar there and finished in 23 steps (Q8:18, Q8:19, Q8:23); and in put-some-mug-on-sidetable the Parent re-opened drawers 1-4 before reaching diningtable (P3:2, P3:8, P3:13, P3:16), while the Candidate went to diningtable first and finished in 4 steps (Q3:1, Q3:4). Across the ten current pairs the Candidate succeeded on 9 and the Parent on 7, and both flips (butterknife-in-drawer, soapbar-in-cabinet) are cases where the Candidate reached a receptacle family the Parent never visited; because the same diff also changed the exact-category rule, this batch-level gain is a joint-intervention result and cannot be attributed to the sweep clause alone.

The family-sweep wording was not reliably followed and did not by itself break the cycling/step-limit failure mode when the exact target was not found. In the current clean-some-butterknife-and-put-it-in-drawer pair the Candidate still cycled among drawers 1-5 and the countertops and reached the 50-step limit, as did the Parent (Q7:45, Q7:47, Q7:49, Q7:50; P7:50). In the current cool-some-apple-and-put-it-in-microwave pair both sides cycled among cabinets, countertops and the fridge before eventually reaching diningtable, and the Candidate used 46 steps versus the Parent's 38 although both succeeded (P10:1, P10:33, P10:38; Q10:40, Q10:46). The simple pairs were unaffected: both sides succeeded on the mug, pencil and clean-soapbar-to-toilet tasks, identically at P4/Q4 and P9/Q9 and with one extra Candidate step at P5/Q5 (P4:4/Q4:4, P5:5/Q5:6, P9:6/Q9:6). So the sweep clause is associated with reaching target-bearing surfaces in some tasks but did not eliminate loopy search or guarantee an exhaustive single pass.

A prior rewrite of the same search step (S1_R05-era) had instead added: include visible open surfaces (tables, countertops, shelves, sidetables) rather than only closed drawers/cabinets; leave an opened receptacle that lacks the target and pick a different uninspected candidate from the current admissible list; do not re-enter a location just left or repeat a short cycle; and prefer a receptacle type not yet tried. Its observed response was mixed: in the clean-butterknife pair both sides cycled among drawers 1-7 and hit the 50-step limit without finding a butterknife, and in the put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet pair both sides cycled among cabinets 1-4, with the Candidate adding two receptacle types the Parent never visited — bathtubbasin 1 (Q8:3) and sinkbasin 2 (Q8:19, Q8:43, Q8:49) — and still reaching the limit. So that wording was followed only in isolated instances and did not break the cycling/step-limit failure when the exact target was absent.

The earlier S1_R03-era search rewrite had added: use current and recent observations to avoid immediate cycling; do not re-examine an already-open empty receptacle or check inventory while carrying nothing; and, when the obvious cabinets/fridge have not yielded the target or the step count is already high, prefer uninspected drawers, shelves, the diningtable, or other listed receptacles and new unopened containers over known-empty locations. Its response was mixed: in one cool-a-bread instance the Parent cycled among the fridge, cabinets and countertops and hit the step limit without finding bread, while the Candidate expanded to the diningtable, took a bread there, cooled it at the fridge and placed it on countertop 1, succeeding; but in another cool-a-bread pair with an identical room the Parent explored countertop 3 and took the bread there while the Candidate never went to countertop 3 and cycled among cabinets, shelves and the fridge to the limit; and in a cool-a-plate pair the Candidate reached the plate in cabinet 9 only at step 49 and exhausted the budget one step later while the Parent finished at step 38. Net task-level outcome that round was slightly lower for the Candidate (6 successes vs 7), within plausible stochastic variation. Thus the anti-cycling/step-budget language was already unreliably followed, with failures concentrated when the exact target was absent.

Two successive strengthenings of the ordinary non-desklamp exact-target rule show the same adherence limit: the rule has not reliably prevented a Candidate from manipulating a near-match object when the exact target is absent, and has not converted such an absent-target failure into success. The S1_R05-era edit required that, when the exact noun phrase had not been observed, the Actor not acquire, clean, cool, heat or place a different but related object; in that round's clean-some-butterknife-and-put-it-in-drawer pair the exact butterknife was absent, drawer 1 held knife 1 and spatula 1, and the Candidate took the near-miss knife, cleaned it and moved it (v23_4_R05_replay_v3_validation_001/P7:2, .../Q7:4, .../P7:8, .../Q7:9, .../Q7:17, .../Q7:19) while both sides reached the 50-step limit. The current diff instead requires confirming an object's exact category name before acquiring, cleaning, cooling, heating or placing it and explicitly names near-matches to reject (knife vs butterknife, soapbottle vs soapbar, cup vs mug, spraybottle vs soapbottle); in the same task this round, drawer 1 again held knife 1 and spatula 1 (P7:2, Q7:4), no butterknife was found in the observed search, and the Candidate again took the near-match knife (Q7:9), cleaned it (Q7:17) and placed it in drawer 1 (Q7:19), as did the Parent (P7:5, P7:7, P7:9); both hit the 50-step limit. In the R05 put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet pair the exact soapbar was also absent and neither side picked up a near-miss, yet both also hit the limit. So the stricter wording neither reliably suppressed near-match manipulation nor produced success where the exact target was not located.

The strengthened exact-category wording coexisted with preserved exact-object selection whenever the requested object was actually present, even when near-matches were co-located. Current evidence: in put-a-clean-butterknife-in-drawer the Candidate reached countertop 2, which displayed knife 1 and knife 2 as well as butterknife 1, and took the exact butterknife (Q6:16, Q6:17), then cleaned and placed it for a success (Q6:21); in put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet the Candidate left cabinet 2's near-match soapbottle 2 and spraybottle 2 untouched (Q8:7, Q8:16) and later took the exact soapbar 1 from shelf 1 (Q8:18, Q8:19), cleaning and placing it (Q8:23); in put-a-clean-soapbar-in-toilet both sides took the exact soapbar 1 while the co-located spraybottle 1 was left (P9:2, Q9:2); and both sides took the exact mug, pencil and apple in the mug, pencil and cool-apple pairs (P3:2/Q3:2, P4:2/Q4:2, P5:3/Q5:4, P10:33/Q10:41). The parallel S1_R05-era observations were the same, with both sides taking the exact mug, pencil and butterknife items (v23_4_R05_replay_v3_validation_001/P3:2, Q3:2, P4:2, Q4:2, P5:3, Q5:4, P6:3, Q6:3). In these observations substitution occurred only when the exact object was not present, but the near-match violation above shows the rule is not reliably binding.

Earlier incarnations of the same no-substitute principle (inside the temperature-conditioned placement guidance of the S1_R03/S1_R04-era edits) were examined when the exact target was absent: in a cool-a-pan task the Parent eventually took and cooled a pot while the Candidate repeatedly saw the pot without taking or moving it; in a heat-a-mug task the Parent took and heated a cup while the Candidate left the visible cup untouched; and in a hot-mug placement task the Parent took cup 2 from the countertop and heated it while the Candidate left the visible cup untouched. All these executions still reached the step limit because the exact pan or mug was not found, so abstention saved substitution steps but produced no success. This preserves the conditional-usefulness limit: the rule can avoid ineffective near-miss manipulation, but its task-level value depends on the exact target existing in an inspectable location, and the later stronger wording does not guarantee adherence either.
